evidence:
anchor.lisp:166-169
(let ((key (fnn-crypto-octets pinned-key nonce-octets "pinned anchor key")))
  (when (/= (length key) nonce-octets)
    (return-from fnn-anchor-acquire '(:fault :pinned-key)))
The ACL2 profile's sixth element is *fn-anchor-nonce-octets* (books/anchor-servers.lisp:72). The key is proved to be *fn-anchor-key-octets* wide (anchor-servers.lisp:89-93), which is a different constant.
fix: Add the key width to the ACL2 profile, or leave the key-width check to ACL2 (fn-anchor-wire-host-parse already takes the pinned key), and drop the nonce-based check.
notes: 10-02 23:07 fixed; ran tests/native_anchor_acquisition-mock.lisp under sbcl (passes) + python source test; pre-network width fault removed, ACL2 refuses :arguments
reviewer: anchor.lisp:166-169 checks the pinned key's length against nonce-octets (the profile's sixth element). The ACL2 key width is the separate *fn-anchor-key-octets* (books/anchor.lisp:86); both it and *fn-anchor-nonce-octets* (line 87) are 32 today, so nothing fails now. This is a latent coupling bug: the host derives a key-width rule from an unrelated constant, and changing the nonce width would break every acquisition with (:fault :pinned-key).
scenario: The check passes only because both constants are currently 32. A move to a 64-octet nonce (the Google Roughtime nonce width) makes every pinned 32-octet Ed25519 key fail this check, so every acquisition reports '(:fault :pinned-key)'. It also contradicts the file's claim that raw Lisp carries no second set of wire-size constants: the host has invented a key-width rule from an unrelated field.
title: Pinned anchor key width is checked against the nonce width
